catalog_quote: 1.4. Stress. Abkhaz is characterized by strong dynamic stress, which can fall on any syllable in polysyllabic words. Longer words can have a secondary stress. Less usually, two syllables in a long word can be equally stressed. Stress distinguishes many otherwise homophonic words and word-forms, cf. áč'a 'quail' – a-č'á 'wheat; bread'; á-la 'eye' – a-lá 'dog'; áħºa 'sword' – a-ħºá 'pig, swine'; á-pa-ra 'to jump' – a-pára 'money' – a-pa-rá 'to knit'. According to Dybo (1989) and Spruit (1986: 37-79), every syllable (including monoconsonantal morphemes) in Abkhaz can be assigned a certain prosodic valence (high or low, or in other terminology, dominant or recessive). It is the combinations of syllables each possessing its own valence, which determine the stress pattern of the given word(-form). According to Dybo, this accentual model could be a transformation of an older tonal system.

new_statements.quote: მახვილი აფხაზურ ენაში ინტენსიური და მოძრავია, ე. ი. მახვილი შეიძლება მოუდიოდეს სიტყვის ნებისმიერ პოზიციაში მდგომ ხმოვანს: სიტყვის თავში – áжәа 'სიტყვა', áшьха 'მთა'..., სიტყვის შუაში – ады́рра 'ცოდნა', ашьáнҵа 'კაჟი'... სიტყვის ბოლოს – аӡы́ 'წყალი', алабá 'ჯოხი'... [...] მრავალი ომონიმური სიტყვა ერთმანეთისაგან სწორედ მახვილის ადგილის მიხედვით განირჩევა: áла 'თვალი' – алá 'ძაღლი', áҕа 'საბერველი' – аҕá 'მტერი', áҳәа 'ხმალი' – аҳәá 'ღორი'... სიტყვათა ერთ ჯგუფში ზოგი აფიქსის დართვა იწვევს მახვილის გადანაცვლებას, მაგრამ იმავე აფიქსთა დართვა სხვა სიტყვათა ჯგუფში არ უცვლის მახვილს ადგილს. ასეთ შემთხვევებში რაიმე კანონზომიერების დადგენა ჭირს.
new_statements.translation: Stress in the Abkhaz language is intensive and mobile, i.e. stress can fall on a vowel standing in any position of the word: at the beginning of the word – áжәа 'word', áшьха 'mountain'..., in the middle of the word – ады́рра 'knowledge', ашьáнҵа 'flint'..., at the end of the word – аӡы́ 'water', алабá 'stick'... [...] Many homonymous words are distinguished from one another precisely by the place of stress: áла 'eye' – алá 'dog', áҕа 'bellows' – аҕá 'enemy', áҳәа 'sword' – аҳәá 'pig'... In one group of words the addition of certain affixes causes a shift of stress, but the addition of the same affixes in another group of words does not change the place of stress. In such cases it is difficult to establish any regularity.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Abkhaz (qs-tier-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so this source fills the gap rather than agreeing or contradicting: stress is free/mobile, non-positional, contrastive, and (per this author) without a statable rule. Compatible with the Dybo's-Rule morphological-accent analyses already held by the project in the same directory (Andersson 2024 diss. pp. 4, 92, 99: obligatory, culminative, contrastive, no window restriction, no weight sensitivity), which agree on the facts but treat placement as predictable from morpheme accent classes.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is 'intensive and mobile': it may fall on the vowel of any syllable (initial, medial or final), it is contrastive (many segmentally identical words are distinguished only by stress position, e.g. eye/dog, bellows/enemy, sword/pig), the same word may sometimes be stressed in two places, and adding a given affix shifts stress in one class of words but not in another; the author says it is hard to establish any regularity. No positional or weight rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: The elided sentence (p. 34) notes that one and the same word may sometimes carry stress in different places: аҵáра | аҵарá 'learning'. Affix-conditioned stress shift occurs in some word groups but not others. p. 36: reduction is very widespread, 'as a result of reduction vowels disappear under the influence of stress' (*амашы́н → амшы́н 'sea', агәáра → агәáр 'fence', áкалаҭ → áклаҭ 'basket'). p. 27: a stressed у in loanwords sometimes stays unchanged.
new_statements.identity_note: Gvantseladze 2003 describes the Abkhaz literary (standard) language ('აფხაზურ სალიტერატურო ენას', p. 27), written in Georgian for Georgian learners; the open copy (125 pp. The two listed works are one and the same book (Georgian and English title renderings).

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Abkhaz (src qs-tier-2026-09-12) carries an empty rule and there are no existing_statements, so there is no placement to agree with or contradict; this work supplies the type: free, mobile, lexically contrastive dynamic stress with morphologically conditioned, irregular shifts. It is consistent with the Andersson 2024/2026 and Wolfe 2000 materials already held by the project from the verification (contrastive lexical accent, no window, no weight sensitivity, placement by morpheme accent specification / Dybo's Rule), which give the formal rule that Gvantseladze says is hard to state.ge link.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Abkhaz has dynamic (intensity) stress that is free and mobile: it can fall on any syllable (initial, medial, final), some words have variant stress placements, stress position alone distinguishes many minimal pairs (áла 'eye' vs алá 'dog'), and affixation shifts stress in some word groups but not others with no regularity the author can state. p. 36 adds that unstressed vowels are frequently deleted (reduction) under the influence of stress (*амашы́н → амшы́н 'sea', áкалаҭ → áклаҭ 'basket').
new_statements.exceptions: Free variation of stress place in some words (аҵáра ~ аҵарá 'study'); affix-induced stress shift applies to some lexical groups and not others ('hard to establish any regularity'); stressed у in loanwords sometimes retained (p. 27); vowel reduction/deletion conditioned by stress (p. 36).
new_statements.identity_note: Gvantseladze 2003 describes standard (literary) Abkhaz as taught to Georgian learners; no particular dialect is singled out in the stress section.

tone_statements.citation: Dybo, V. A. 2007. Zapadnokavkazskaja akcentologičeskaja rekonstrukcija [West Caucasian accentological reconstruction]. In: Lingvističeskaja komparativistika v kul'turnom i istoričeskom aspektax, 88-113. Moskva: Izdatel'stvo Moskovskogo universiteta. (pages/publisher per Borise 2021 reference list; inslav.ru offprint PDF, 26 pp.)
tone_statements.quote: Три дочерних системы — абхазская, тапантская и убыхская — сохранили все её основные (системообразущие) параметры … дочерние западнокавказские акцентные системы … могут демонстрироваться как образцы «чистой» парадигматической акцентной системы. Эта их особенность вызывала недоверие к чисто акцентному их характеру, чтó привело к ряду проверок с целью обнаружить сохранение тонового их основания. Проверка бзыбского состояния, проведенная С. А. Старостиным, привела к отрицательным результатам, в тапантском диалекте ему как будто удалось обнаружить слабые тоны.
tone_statements.translation: The three daughter systems - Abkhaz, Tapanta and Ubykh - have preserved all its basic (system-forming) parameters ... the daughter West Caucasian accent systems ... can be exhibited as specimens of a 'pure' paradigmatic accent system. This peculiarity of theirs aroused distrust of their purely accentual character, which led to a series of checks aimed at finding a preserved tonal basis. The check of the Bzyb state carried out by S. A. Starostin gave negative results; in the Tapanta dialect he apparently managed to find weak tones.
tone_statements.summary: No tone: Abkhaz is a purely accentual system with mobile stress; a check of the Bzyb dialect for a surviving tonal basis was negative (weak tones perhaps in Tapanta Abaza).

tone_statements.citation: Dybo, V. A., S. L. Nikolayev & S. A. Starostin. 1978. A tonological hypothesis on the origin of paradigmatic accent systems. In: Estonian Papers in Phonetics 1978, 16-20. Tallinn: Academy of Sciences of the Estonian S.S.R., Institute of Language and Literature.
tone_statements.quote: The evolution of the Abkhazo-Adyg tonal system may consequently be presented in the following way: Stage 1. Existence of tonal oppositions relevant for every syllable. ... At the end of this the first reading system develops, in which tonal oppositions become relevant only on the stressed syllable, but are already neutralised in other syllables. Such a system is to be seen in the Abaza language. Stage 3. The final loss of tonal oppositions, thus giving rise to a "pure" system of paradigmatic accent. Such a system is characteristic for Abkhazian and, to judge from descriptions and texts, for Oubykh.
tone_statements.summary: No synchronic tone; free paradigmatic (valency-based) stress; dominant/recessive valencies reconstructed as *H/*L syllable tones (tonal origin hypothesis).

tone_statements.citation: Dybo, Vladimir A. 1977. Zapadnokavkazskaja akcentnaja sistema i problema eë proisxoždenija [The West Caucasian accentual system and the problem of its origin]. In: Konferencija 'Nostratičeskie jazyki i nostratičeskoe jazykoznanie'. Tezisy dokladov, 41-45. Moskva: Institut slavjanovedenija i balkanistiki AN SSSR. (86 pp; ed. board Vjač. Vs. Ivanov et al.)
tone_statements.quote: 7. Типологически рассмотренная акцентная система наиболее близка к тональным системам с механическим правилом постановки иктуса на последнем слоге первой платформы тонов высшего регистра. В связи с этим можно думать, что западнокавказская акцентная система возникла из тональной системы подобного типа в результате падения тональных различий и фонологизации акцентного контура, сопутствовавшего этим тональным характеристикам.
tone_statements.translation: 7. Typologically, the accent system examined is closest to tonal systems with a mechanical rule placing the ictus on the last syllable of the first platform of higher-register tones. In this connection one may think that the West Caucasian accent system arose from a tonal system of this type as a result of the loss of tonal distinctions and the phonologization of the accentual contour that accompanied these tonal characteristics.
tone_statements.summary: Abkhaz is described with mobile word stress placed by morpheme valency, not tone; the author derives this accent system historically from a lost tonal system (tonal distinctions fell away).

sources.quote: В абхазском языке ударение динамическое, интенсивное, не фиксированное; áлагара 'начать', агы́лара 'вставать', анапы́ 'рука', [4th example, harvest: illegible in scan] 'урожай'. Слова или те или иные формы одного и того же слова весьма часто разнятся между собой только по месту ударения, например: áла 'глаз', алá 'собака'; áцəа 'сон', ацəá 'кожа', абáра 'сухое место', абарá 'сохнуть' и т. д. Такое противопоставление слов или форм по месту ударения есть в большинстве случаев результат различного морфологического и лексического состава указанных основ. В абхазском языке ударение подвижное: в одной и той же именной и глагольной основе оно может передвигаться с одного слога на другой в зависимости от формообразования и формоизменения. Более устойчивым в этом отношении является ударение, падающее на слог, который находится в середине основы. [Earlier on the same page:] Для исходного состояния было характерно полногласие. Скопление согласных — результат действия сильного ударения: безударные гласные а, ы (при наличии сильного ударения соседнего слога) редуцировались: амш < *а-ма-ша ... [p. 103:] Гласный ы обычно является ударным; безударный ы характеризуется определенной факультативность

sources.quote: Три дочерних системы — абхазская, тапантская и убыхская — сохранили все её основные (системообразущие) параметры … дочерние западнокавказские акцентные системы … могут демонстрироваться как образцы «чистой» парадигматической акцентной системы. tone.translation: The three daughter systems - Abkhaz, Tapanta and Ubykh - have preserved all its basic (system-forming) parameters ... the daughter West Caucasian accent systems ... can be exhibited as specimens of a 'pure' paradigmatic accent system. This peculiarity of theirs aroused distrust of their purely accentual character, which led to a series of checks aimed at finding a preserved tonal basis. The check of the Bzyb state carried out by S. A. Starostin gave negative results; in the Tapanta dialect he apparently managed to find weak tones.
tone.summary: No tone: Abkhaz is a purely accentual system with mobile stress; a check of the Bzyb dialect for a surviving tonal basis was negative (weak tones perhaps in Tapanta Abaza).

sources.citation: Dybo, V. A., S. L. Nikolayev & S. A. Starostin. 1978. A tonological hypothesis on the origin of paradigmatic accent systems. In: Estonian Papers in Phonetics 1978, 16-20. Tallinn: Academy of Sciences of the Estonian S.S.R., Institute of Language and Literature.
sources.quote: The evolution of the Abkhazo-Adyg tonal system may consequently be presented in the following way: Stage 1. Existence of tonal oppositions relevant for every syllable. ... At the end of this the first reading system develops, in which tonal oppositions become relevant only on the stressed syllable, but are already neutralised in other syllables. Such a system is to be seen in the Abaza language. Stage 3. The final loss of tonal oppositions, thus giving rise to a "pure" system of paradigmatic accent. Such a system is characteristic for Abkhazian and, to judge from descriptions and texts, for Oubykh.
sources.note: No tonal oppositions in Abkhaz: a 'pure' paradigmatic accent (an earlier reading set by +/- syllable valencies; authors' field-work). Syllable tones reconstructed for the proto-language only; Abaza keeps high/low.

Типологически рассмотренная акцентная система наиболее близка к тональным системам с механическим правилом постановки иктуса на последнем слоге первой платформы тонов высшего регистра. tone.translation: 7. Typologically, the accent system examined is closest to tonal systems with a mechanical rule placing the ictus on the last syllable of the first platform of higher-register tones. In this connection one may think that the West Caucasian accent system arose from a tonal system of this type as a result of the loss of tonal distinctions and the phonologization of the accentual contour that accompanied these tonal characteristics.

tone.quote: In Abkhaz and Abaza, stress is predominantly conditioned by morphological factors, though this conditioning is highly intricate. Dybo (1977: 45) and Dybo et al. (1978: 17) hypothesize that the stress properties of NWC languages could have arisen from a tonal system. … it has been observed that Abkhaz and Abaza stress is based on intensity and not pitch movement or vowel duration, but this has not been verified instrumentally (Genko 1955: 63; Tabulova 1976: 39; Arshba 1979: 7). For the languages in which stress is described as primarily cued by pitch/tone, see Borise-tone (this volume).

sources.note: Second-hand (Borise 2021 Word Stress preprint p. 16): 'a metrical analysis by Trigo (1992), which breaks Dybo's Law into three separate rules (here, accented syllable = dominant, unaccented = recessive): 1. Default Accentuation.. right-headed unbounded foot on line-0.. 2. Accent Deletion.. 3. Word Stress: construct a left-headed word foot on line-1', with extrametrical recessive monosyllabic stems and infixal NEG/CAUS; i.e. accents are formalised as metrical grid marks, not tones; Andersson 2026 cites pp. 204, 226, 229.
